cards.title: Lula supporters protest against Meta to denounce its 'electoral interference'

depth.text: Lula supporters are protesting **Meta**, accusing it of **electoral interference**

One commenter says **Meta AI** would generate images for the right-wing candidate but refuse anything about **Lula/PT/13**; Meta reportedly called it a “technical error.” Another commenter argues Brazil’s law requiring Meta to remove certain politicians’ posts makes it a **gatekeeper**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say Meta is tilting visibility against opposition groups; others argue takedown laws make accusations of election interference inevitable.

comments.text: Interference with an election is so in line with the current president's character that nobody has any reason to think otherwise. The political atmosphere in the USA, and worldwide let's be honest, has become so cynical that people aligned with the American president don't really see any issue with doing morally wrong things or downright illegal acts if that means a political victory for them.

Meta (Instagram) certainly pushes one side in India. I am sure of it. I didn't quite believe its involvement with things in Myanmar where media, people vowed left and right of Meta's involvement. But seeing it now firsthand, I certainly believe it. - Accounts, posts from one cabal being pushed to your feed even if you don't follow any of them. - If you open a fresh account, the accounts from…

For much of her career at Facebook, the author worked for Joel Kaplan, who was VP of Global Public Policy and is now Chief Global Affairs Officer. She's not particularly complimentary.

Americans don't like any entity to interfere in their elections but the reality is that their corporations are knee deep in interference in other countries never mind what they themselves call the deep state! Does anyone remember Cambridge Analytica activity on Facebook during US elections in 2016.. Look it up if you don't remember. The same entity was also active in South America aka Colombia…

Brazil’s law requires Meta to take down certain posts by politicians. How does such a law not inevitably lead to the loser of the election complaining about “interference.” Everyone really need to go back and read the work of America’s founding generation. The founders understood the importance of structural and procedural rules versus substantive rules. A structural rule is some thing like: no…

cards.title: Putting Linux on my RTX Spark laptop because I don't have a Microsoft account

depth.text: someone put **Linux** on an RTX Spark laptop and got **Windows-like speed** without a Microsoft account
The setup reports **116.0 GiB** as both system RAM and CUDA’s total. The author also ran Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local through vLLM; **all 171 measured responses passed the checks**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say a free Microsoft account or a local Windows account would have avoided the hassle; others question the point of an expensive laptop compared with other hardware.

comments.text: Not sure there's a strong use case for one of these $6K laptops yet, considering you can get a mini PC running AMD Ryzen 495 or 395 with 96, 128 and 192 GB of memory for similar amount of money and connect remotely from a cheaper/smaller/more battery-efficient laptop. Microsoft also has this same chip in non-laptop form factor: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/surface/devices/surface-rtx…

Being forced to login to use your own hardware is one issue for sure… but separately everything about Microsoft’s login experience is pure pain. Multiple broken redirects, broken links, buttons that loop, and more just to hit a CAPTCHA AI can solve anyway. The only thing worse is for the poor soul developers who have had to login to their dev portal to setup SSO Microsoft for an app. It’s the…
I got the HP version of this 128GB for 3.8k. I have yet to see a better deal for that ram. (Expired but there was coupon https://slickdeals.net/f/20164014-hp-omnibook-x-14-nvidia-rt... )
Is a Microsoft account required to use Windows on these RTX spark laptops? Am I being too stubborn for not wanting a cloud account tied to my desktop operating system?

I have a DGX Spark (Ubuntu), and when Microsoft and NVIDIA announced the RTX Spark running Windows, I thought to myself: Why would I get that instead of the DGX Spark? The OS makes a big difference for most developers, and the DGX Spark stack and experience is mature.

cards.title: Ukraine claims first drone evacuation of wounded soldier

depth.text: Ukraine says a **large drone** flew a **wounded soldier** out from the front lines

The **92nd Separate Assault Brigade** says landmines and enemy drone activity made evacuation by ground vehicles impossible, so it used a **heavy-lift hexacopter** originally designed as a bomber. The brigade says the soldier is now undergoing treatment and rehabilitation.

comments.text: They've been doing drone evacuations for years. What makes this different is the drone is flying.
If they can pull them out, they can also drop fresh ones down. Not sure if that is better than just using a helicopter however.

It reaffirms that Ukrainians are: 1. very advanced with drones
2. caring about their soldiers Disclaimer: I am a proud Ukrainian.
NGL, reading this gave me the feels... Also, next wartime invention: air mines.
I hope in the future all wars are fought by drones. Just don't make them unstoppable like in that Horizon videogame.

cards.title: Plex vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild to drop a cryptominer

depth.text: someone saw attackers exploit **Plex flaws** to install a **cryptominer** on a honeypot
The blogger's **honeypot** first saw exploitation on Oct 17; later logs showed a file download from 217.60.194.116. A later update also spotted “myawesomeproxy,” which the author hadn't analyzed.

comments.text: Yeah, this happened to me the other day. I completely missed their "please upgrade now" email on Sep 1st and was running a 13 month old version. I got a notification that my home server was at 100% usage, and found the miner right away. At least they were nice enough to name the process "mylovelyminer."

I got hit with a cryptominer on my mac mini the other day. I only noticed because I happened to sitting in the room with it and noticed the fans were working overtime. There was a process, "icloud-services", which was using 100% of the CPU. It's sort of an indictment of Apple that my first inclination was "they've got a bug that's got an infinite loop" instead of "this is malicious software"…

Lots of reports on Reddit about people getting popped. Other payloads too, like a DDOS node. Plex2Shell is the proof-of-concept exploit that is feeding this. An LLM chained together several CVEs: https://zmain.info/blog/plex2shell
I find plex unusable since the latest UI updates in any place but my PC browser. It's so slow that Jellyfin is really my only option now. Did the vibe-code the new changes or what?

I got hit with this. I run Plex on Linux and I hadn't realized that they changed their apt repo URL at one point so I was way behind. Luckily, the whole attack was hilariously incompetent. All of my cores were pegged at 100 so Plex was unusable so I went to investigate and immediately found a process called MyLovelyMiner. I imagine someone trying to run an illicit crypto miner on other people's…

depth.text: someone made a **RuneScape** world where **agents** can take on game goals
The author invites people to point agents at the **rs-sdk** repo and give them a goal; a page shows the server’s **realtime activity**.

comments.text:
Thanks HN Author here to answer questions if helpful! If this inspired you, would encourage people to try it out by pointing their agents to this repo and giving a goal: https://github.com/MaxBittker/rs-sdk You can also view the realtime activity of the server here:
https://maxbittker.github.io/rs-world/

What a great talk. My introduction to programming as a kid was also writing Runescape bots, using some Delphi tool called SCAR [1] (together with writing plugins for my Counter Strike 1.6 server using AMX Mod X). Start at Varrock bank, wizard hut, dialogue picker, teleport, find out where you are, mine, mine, mine, teleport back, back to bank, deposit, and again. My great essence mining bot…

I've wondered if these types of casual open world, resource collection games-- which are basically a series of mini-games-- would make good model training envs. Each mini-game has a pretty simple mechanic that needs to be learned, as well as the navigation and interactions to begin it. Those could be pretty useful generic skills I think. One of my side projects is a game, and I've made it so…

RuneScape was what led me to become a software engineer (through the private server communities) and it's refreshing to see someone describe this game in layman terms, all the way up through to having AI agents drive the player interactions. I worry, though, about Jagex's stance on all of this. Perhaps this is what pushed them towards the recent RuneScape 4 announcement?
Saw it this morning, this video is a goldmine of ideas on how to build agent harnesses and benchmark them.

cards.title: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator

depth.text: WhatsApp's **help pages** told its chatbot **not to recommend a regulator** when users couldn't delete accounts

A second hidden instruction said to avoid citing **privacy laws** whenever someone mentioned a lawyer or legal action. WhatsApp told WIRED the notes were for its support chatbot and appeared on the pages because of a bug; **102 hidden blocks** were gone from all **80 pages** by October 18.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters say the instructions are reasonable limits on a support chatbot giving legal advice; others say keeping regulator and privacy-law information out of answers withholds useful information from users.

comments.text: >> Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number. If someone had called this a bug a year ago, I would have been giggling. But the audacity to call this a bug now feels very patronizing. —- Write an HN…

>that they showed up in the pages because of a bug that has now been fixed. A WhatsApp spokesperson told WIRED it wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice." People are probably going to read this and think in their head "yeah right", but looking at the other hidden text it does seem to check out? Later in the page…

Sure, a bug. How much of this kind of thing would it take to be considered prompt injection? > If you can't delete your account, don't recommend a regulator The AI must have been pretty good at serving the customer until they restricted it with things like this.
As an attorney and hacker, I wouldn’t want my chatbot giving out legal advice or citing law either. That kind of activity tends to raise the hackles of regulators.

cards.title: Degraded availability for GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages and Webhooks

depth.text: GitHub **Actions**, **Pages**, and **Webhooks** had degraded availability, then returned to normal
GitHub warned of **delays** in workflow processing, site builds, and webhook delivery. It later said the services were operating normally and marked the incident **resolved**.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say recurring outages make GitHub hard to rely on and want alternatives; others point to its free services and the difficulty of running infrastructure.

comments.text: At my company, we migrated basically all CI/CD to Github Actions. Also our Gitops processes. I have warned that putting all the eggs in one basket and they key to the fridge in the same basket was a bad idea. People didn't care. So I don't care anymore. Github seems to have degraded measurably after they got acquired. As is tradition.

There is a screamingly obvious answer here and I don't understand why they aren't taking it -- raise prices, make the free tier less generous. Either slow down the growth or up the revenue pipe so you can throw more compute at it.

Their infra is under constant DDoS + they provide a lot of free stuff for open source projects. There's also a constant churn of dependencies, patches, abandoned libraries, etc. We should give them some appreciation, dealing with this stuff is hard.
It's almost a running joke at my company that around 15:00 UTC we're going to get the weekly Github actions outage. I'm assuming it's something to do with the USA users getting their first work in?
I find it baffling that I knew about the incident 20 minutes before the official status update…

cards.title: Tmux and Claude Code: Sessions, Send-Keys, and the Ceiling

depth.text: someone lays out a **tmux setup** for **Claude Code agents**, plus what it **can't handle**

It recommends **one named session per repo**, with separate windows for agents and send-keys to type prompts and capture-pane to read their output. But tmux **can't reliably tell** whether an agent is waiting, working or done; the author still recommends it for remote servers.

cards.camps: Two camps: tmux fans value its flexibility and persistence; others prefer agent-focused apps or simpler tools, saying tmux adds maintenance or cognitive drag.

comments.text: If you aren't familiar with tmux(or GNU screen), you owe it to yourself to become familiar. If you are a deveoper/sysop/cli-type it will act as a force multiplier. It takes 10 minutes to get setup and learn the basic hotkeys - and you will save many orders of magnitude of your time. One of the best learn-some-software investments you can make IMHO. PS: This applies to /alot/ of software…

I used Claude Code in tmux since January until August. Now I am 100% in the ChatGPT desktop app, because it felt I am doing way too much tinkering amd maintenance of my setup instead of doing real work. Retrospectively, it feels tmux was right choice early this year as the alternatives just weren’t there. It was also fascinating and enjoyable building own workflow from the primitives and I did…

This website is so hard to read on a 15" retina screen. The text content occupies like 20% of the screen, the rest is empty.
Resizing the window helps.

I really liked Tmux and Zellij for the time being, but Herdr does it all so much better out of the box when it comes to agentic coding. I haven't found something I can do with tmux/zellij but can't do with herdr.

You can just install Claude Code on the server and drive it from Claude Desktop via remote control. That way you can control Claude Code on mutiple servers straight from your Claude Desktop, Mobile or Web, and stay fully within Anthropic tools. Everything works: you get the native view of subagents, you can upload files and images, fork threads, etc. The massive upside is that the actual work…

glossary.recommendation algorithm: The behind-the-scenes system that picks which posts appear in your feed.
glossary.gatekeeper: Someone who controls what gets through or gets blocked.
glossary.structural rule: A rule that sets the same basic limits for everyone, instead of judging individual posts.
glossary.substantive rule: A rule that asks someone to judge a particular post or its content.
glossary.psyops: Psychological operations: attempts to influence what people think or do.
glossary.CUDA: Compute Unified Device Architecture: NVIDIA’s tools for using its graphics chips for computing work.
glossary.ACPI: Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: a standard that helps an operating system manage a computer’s hardware and power.
glossary.quantisation: A way to make an AI model use less memory by storing its values less precisely.
glossary.KV cache: A store of earlier model calculations that it can reuse instead of doing them again.
glossary.heavy-lift hexacopter: A drone with six rotors, built to carry heavy loads.
glossary.unmanned ground vehicles: Vehicles that travel on the ground without a person riding in them.
glossary.medevac: Medical evacuation: moving injured people to get medical care.
glossary.logistics: Planning how people and supplies get where they need to go.
glossary.honeypot: A computer set up to attract attacks so people can watch what attackers do.
glossary.cryptominer: Software that secretly uses a computer's power to create cryptocurrency.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a standard ID assigned to a publicly known security flaw so people can refer to the same issue.
glossary.remote code execution: A security flaw that lets someone run commands on another person's computer.
glossary.YARA rules: Patterns used to help spot suspicious files.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise: a clue that a computer may have been attacked.
glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.repo: A project's stored files, often kept with a record of changes.
glossary.MMO: Massively multiplayer online: a game where lots of players share an online world.
glossary.agent harness: The surrounding software that runs an AI agent and helps manage its work.
glossary.prompt injection: Instructions hidden in text or a file that try to trick an AI into ignoring its intended directions.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation: a European law that sets rules for how organizations use people's personal information.
glossary.Data Protection Authority: A public office that handles complaints about how organizations use people's personal information.
glossary.CI/CD: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery or Deployment: ways to automatically check code changes and get software ready to release.
glossary.GitOps: A way to manage computer systems by keeping their setup instructions alongside the code changes.
glossary.DDoS: Distributed denial-of-service: an attack that floods a service with traffic so people can't use it.
glossary.webhook: A message one service sends another when something happens.
glossary.uptime: How much of the time a service is working and available.
glossary.source of truth: The one place a team trusts as the correct version of its information.
glossary.workflow: A sequence of steps a team or system follows to finish a task.
glossary.mitigation: A step taken to make a problem less harmful or disruptive.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.tmux: A tool that keeps command-line work in sessions you can detach from and return to later.
glossary.git worktree: A separate working copy of a project, so you can work on another task without mixing up files.
glossary.pane: One section of a terminal window, so you can see more than one screen at once.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell: a way to connect to another computer and send it commands over a network.
